newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban say ready for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban say ready for peace talks.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia said on Monday it was ready for peace talks with opposition forces that it has been battling north of Kabul.

"We don't have any objection to peace talks if (General Abdul Rashid) Dostum and (Ahmad Shah) Masood say now that they are ready for a ceasefire, an exchange of prisoners of war and holding of further talks," Amir Khan Mutaqi, the Taleban's acting minister for Information and Culture, told reporters.
Last week the Taleban launched an offensive against Dostum and Masood just one day after U.N.-sponsored peace talks adjourned in Islamabad without any apparent progress.
The Taleban took the Soviet-built Bagram airbase, the town of Charikar, about 50 km (31 miles) north of Kabul, and much of Kapisa province, amid reports of disunity in opposition ranks.
Mutaqi again rejected the opposition demand for the demilitarisation of Kabul, seized by the Islamic militia last September, saying police already controlled the city.

"The demilitarisation of Mazar-i-Sharif will solve the difficulty," he said with a smile, referring to the northern city under Dostum's control. "There is no problem in Kabul. It is peaceful and it is irrational to demilitarise it."
Mutaqi said there had been no change at the front lines north of Kabul since Friday, adding that Taleban fighters were disarming villagers in the districts they captured last week.
Military analysts blamed a lack of coordination between Masood and Dostum, old rivals who joined forces only after the fall of Kabul, for the latest opposition setbacks.
"Differences among the anti-Taleban groups caused the fall of several areas to Taleban", said one analyst.
"Each one wanted to have overall command of front-line activities and the dislike of local (ethnic Tajik) people for Dostum's fighters was a major factor in the Taleban victories."
Dostum's mainly ethnic Uzbek troops are allied with Masood's Tajik fighters and a Shi'ite Moslem faction against the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, most of whom come from the south.
The analyst, who asked not to be named, said Tajik villagers had accused Dostum's men of various incidents of looting and attempted rape, causing friction and revenge killings.

Witnesses who visited the opposition side of the front line said they had seen dozens of unarmed Dostum soldiers heading with their sleeping bags for the Salang Tunnel, at the head of a Hindu Kush mountain pass guarding Dostum's northern heartland.
They said the front lines were not properly manned and Masood's fighters were thin on the ground.
"These could all be signs of gradual damage to the alliance which may lead to it falling apart," the analyst said.
